3. Scripts: Precision Spell Modifications
Scripts are advanced magical notations that allow spellcasters—primarily Arcanists—to alter the 
properties of spells with surgical precision. They function as one-time enhancements, modifying how a 
spell is cast or what it does. These changes are pre-written on arcane parchments or embedded into 
spellbooks, offering controlled flexibility without breaking the core rules of magic.
What Is a Script?
A script is a magical overlay—a pre-written set of arcane instructions that alter a single spell in real time 
when cast. Unlike spontaneous casting or metamagic, scripts require preparation, materials, and 
knowledge to use.
•Single-use scripts are consumed when cast.
•Stored scripts can be recorded into a spellbook and reused (at the cost of new materials).
Creating a Script
Only trained spellcrafters (typically Arcanists or those with the Scriptcraft perk) can design scripts. These 
casters use enchanted ink, glyphic geometry, and knowledge of magical syntax to write safe, functional 
modifications.
Requirements:
•Access to Scriptcraft.
•Scribing Tools (enchanted ink, parchment, and glyph guides).
•Time & Cost:
◦ 1 day per spell level (common spells).
◦ 2 days per spell level (rare or modified spells).
◦ 25 CR per spell level in materials.
•Skill Check:
◦ Arcana check: DC 15 + Spell Level.
▪ Failure: The script is flawed; using it causes a backfire or uncontrolled magic.
▪ Success: The script is viable and stable.
▪ Enhanced Success (5+ over DC): The script is especially efficient—costs 10% less to cast or is 
quicker to activate.
Using a Script
A prepared script is cast in conjunction with a base spell. The spellcaster reads the modifications aloud or 
channels them through a glyph, causing the spell to follow the scriptʼs commands.
Casting a Scripted Spell:
•Consumes the script parchment unless scripted into a spellbook.
•Requires no extra action to cast but adds +1 Resonance DC due to complexity.
•A failed spell (due to counterspell or fumble) still consumes the script.

7.3 🗣  Serpent Language: Psychogloss
Serpents do not speak in words—they resonate. Their language, called Psychogloss, is a directed 
harmonic broadcast composed of emotional packets, image clusters, and synchronized pulses.
•Understanding: Only species with psychic capacity, trained emotional attunement, or implanted 
translators can perceive Psychogloss directly.
•Translation Difficulty: Psychogloss lacks exact tense or tone—it communicates intention and 
trajectory rather than past/present distinctions. “I forgive you” and “I intend to forgive you if 
conditions align” may sound identical to untrained ears.
•Written Form: Serpents sometimes inscribe resonant spirals, a calligraphic psychic glyph pattern that 
activates memories or sensations upon viewing. These are only safely readable by Serpents or those 
trained in empathic shielding.
Roleplay Note:
Players choosing to speak in Psychogloss should describe the feeling, imagery, or emotional context of 
their message. For example:
“I pulse a coil of warm regret tinged with amber serenity—implying shared sorrow without blame.”
7.4 ⚠  Species Restrictions and Roleplaying Guidance
❗  Power Balance and Setting Fit
Due to their powerful passive effects and narrative weight, Serpents are not ideal for casual or early-tier 
campaigns. GMs should consider:
•Limiting Serpent characters to advanced, political, or fringe-infiltration storylines.
•Treating Serpent PCs as rare, with unique story consequences tied to their identity.
•Balancing by increasing social resistance, cultural prejudice, or political complications.
🧠  Narrative Responsibility
Serpent characters are emotionally invasive by nature. Players should:
•Discuss boundaries for psychic/emotional manipulation with their group.
•Avoid using Dissonance in ways that remove other playersʼ agency or enjoyment.
•Treat the Serpentʼs presence as a narrative tension, not a tool for domination.
🌍  Social Interaction
Even when dampened, a Serpentʼs presence causes discomfort. In most worlds:
•NPCs may flinch, distrust, or defer to Serpent characters.

Arborae culture is ancient, layered, and deeply shaped by their ecological origins and spiritual

during religious upheaval, their memory endures in scattered ruins and whispered legends.
Over time, the Tree Courts replaced the mineral order, forming a complex network of culturally distinct 
houses. Each tree species represented a philosophy and biome, with regional high courts and local low 
courts forming the backbone of Arborae governance. These courts were religious as much as political—
rooted in the belief that each tree type held divine traits worthy of reverence and societal guidance.
The rise of Cipra, an early treewalker who could pass between realities using sacred trees, disrupted 
this ancient system. As Cipra brought alien trees and new magics to Arbor-IV, his followers formed the 
Cipraic faith, which overthrew the old order during the Dark Winter Era. The early Sons of the Trees
suppressed old gods and established a near-theocratic regime based on treewalking, ecological 
expansion, and sacred stewardship.
After centuries of corruption and overreach, the Cipraic regime collapsed in the Holy Wars, ushering in 
the Winter-Spring Revival, where new sects and spiritual factions emerged. Among them, the Sons and 
Daughters of Ash and Elm rose to prominence, representing a more conservative, sometimes 
nationalistic strain of belief. Radical offshoots of this group, collectively referred to as the Nafa, led the 
courts during the Goblin invasion of Havalaea and are remembered for authoritarian policies and

deeper still in the soil.

A macro is a magical construct written with sigils—glyphs that encode conditions, activators, and timing. 
These allow multiple spells to function together like a program, making magic behave more like a system 
than a single effect.
Macros can:
•Chain spells in specific sequences.

•Cast multiple spells simultaneously (with cost).
•Share spells across multiple casters.
Macros are limited by complexity, and each additional spell increases both the difficulty and Resonance 
risk.

Creating a macro involves combining spells and embedding them with runes that control sequence, 
timing, and interaction.

In keeping with Multiversalʼs XP-driven system:

culture, history, power structures, and lived-in realism. A well-designed civilization feels like it exists

🏛  Building Societies That Feel Organic and Lived-In
A civilization should feel cohesive and evolving, not just a static backdrop. Consider:
✔  Cultural Identity – What defines this society? Traditions, customs, or philosophies?
✔  Language & Communication – Is there a common tongue? Multiple dialects? Telepathic networks?
✔  Economy & Trade – How do they sustain themselves? What resources are abundant or scarce?
✔  Art & Entertainment – What pastimes, storytelling methods, and artistic expressions exist?
✔  Daily Life & Routine – What does an average citizen's day look like?
✔  Inter-Civilization Relations – Do they interact through diplomacy, trade, war, or isolation?
📌  Worldbuilding Tip: Societies evolve—old traditions fade, new ideas take hold. Think about what has 
changed over time.
🔮  The Role of Magic vs. Technology in Civilizational Development
How a civilization advances depends on whether it prioritizes magic, technology, or a hybrid of both.
󰩃  Magic-Dominant Societies
✔  Magic replaces technology (e.g., floating cities, enchanted tools, teleportation hubs).
✔  Social status may depend on magical ability (mage aristocracy vs. mundane working class).
✔  Magic may be regulated by guilds, deities, or traditions.
🤖  Tech-Dominant Societies
✔  Scientific advancement leads to space travel, AI governance, or cybernetic augmentation.
✔  Energy sources define progress—fusion, antimatter, or renewable tech?
✔  Societal control: Is AI running the government? Are corporations more powerful than nations?
⚖  Hybrid Societies
✔  Magic and technology co-exist (e.g., techno-magic, bioengineering enhanced by arcane energy).
✔  Tension between magic users and technologists—are they allies or rivals?
✔  Magic is mechanized—factory-produced spells, or artificial mages?
📌  Worldbuilding Tip: The level of advancement must feel consistent—if one faction has starships

Homebrewing Rules and Game Mechanics
Homebrewing allows GMs and players to modify existing mechanics or introduce new ones to better 
suit their campaignʼs needs. While it provides exciting opportunities for customization, it requires 
careful balance to maintain game integrity and avoid unintended power imbalances.
Identifying What to Modify in an Existing System
Before implementing homebrew changes, itʼs essential to identify which mechanics require modification 
and why.
•Assess Pain Points – Determine if a rule slows down gameplay, creates imbalance, or doesnʼt fit the 
campaignʼs themes.
•Gather Player Feedback – If multiple players express frustration with a mechanic, it may warrant 
modification.
•Clarify the Goal – Ensure that modifications enhance gameplay rather than complicating it 
unnecessarily.
📌  GM Tip: If a rule is frequently ignored, altered, or avoided, consider revising it for better usability and 
engagement.
Balancing Custom Mechanics to Avoid Game Breakage
Balancing homebrew content ensures that new mechanics donʼt overshadow existing ones or break the 
gameʼs internal logic.
•Compare to Existing Mechanics – Use official rules as a baseline for damage, effects, and 
limitations.
•Avoid Excessive Power Creep – New abilities should provide interesting choices, not automatic 
superiority.
•Introduce Trade-Offs – If a mechanic provides a powerful benefit, ensure it comes with appropriate 
costs or limitations.
•Ensure Progression Balance – Consider how homebrew mechanics scale over time to avoid sudden 
power spikes.
📌  GM Tip: If a homebrew mechanic feels too strong, consider adjusting its resource cost, requiring a 
higher skill check, or adding situational restrictions to keep it balanced.
Designing Homebrew Spells, Feats, and Abilities
Creating custom content can add depth to your game, but it should align with existing mechanics to 
maintain balance.
•Spells – Compare new spells to existing ones of the same level and spell school. Ensure damage 
scaling and utility are reasonable.
•Feats – Provide unique, situational benefits rather than all-encompassing power boosts.
